paper.paper_scope: Examines work hardening of polycrystalline Fe–Al alloys spanning from nearly pure Fe up to ~40 at.% Al (present experimental alloys 15–35 at.% Al, plus 0.1% B additions), combining room-temperature compression testing with TEM analysis of dislocation structures to explain the sharp work-hardening peak near 28% Al.
paper.title: Work hardening in Fe–Al alloys

processes.description: Induction melted in an alumina crucible under inert gas, drop cast into a 25 mm diameter Cu mould (grain size ~0.25 mm) with sufficiently slow cooling to develop a high degree of B2 order for Al-rich alloys and good DO3 order for 25–30% Al; compression samples were then tested at room temperature to 2–3% strain at a nominal strain rate of 3×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, and thin foils were prepared from the centre of the deformed samples for TEM.
processes.processes_notes: The same processing/testing route was applied to all eight alloys; the resulting state of order (disordered, B2 or DO3) is determined by alloy composition and the (common) slow cooling rather than by a separate process. alloy_id is left null because this single terminal state applies to all alloys in the study.

unmapped_findings: Work hardening rate, measured over 1–1.5% strain, shows a sharp peak for alloys containing 26–30 at.% Al, with the maximum observed anywhere in the 26–29% Al range (b0012, b0029).
The study combines literature data (from essentially pure Fe up to the intermetallic FeAl with 40% Al) with new experimental alloys spanning 15–35% Al (b0011, b0012, b0062).
Addition of 0.1% B to the alloys led to only a slight increase in flow stress relative to B-free samples, with little consistent change in the work hardening rate (b0029).
Two literature data points correspond to Fe–Al alloys containing about 0.1% B (b0015).
No APB tubes were observed after deformation, giving little support to the APB-tube-based work-hardening model (b0049, b0052).

A dislocation reaction between two <111> superdislocations on different {110} glide planes produces a pair of sessile <100> edge dislocations on cube planes (e.g., [111] + [1-11] → pair of [100] edge dislocations along [010] in a (001) plane), acting as locks near 28–30% Al (b0039, b0059, b0065).

The elastic anisotropy factor peaks at 25–30% Al (Fe3Al region); the work hardening peak coincides with this anisotropy peak, but the effect is attributed to core/Peierls effects rather than elastic anisotropy itself (b0018, b0054, b0058, b0064).

Dislocation structures show a transition from single bowed dislocations for disordered materials (15–20% Al) to paired superdislocations with straight screw segments for highly ordered materials (28–35% Al); DO3-ordered Fe–25% Al retains single dislocations trailing shear APB because APB energies are too low (b0063).
No evidence was found for the operation of coupled four-partial dislocations that would constitute the perfect superdislocation for the DO3-ordered state (b0052, b0063).
